interactions.summary: After a student tries to rescue the judge model, Jiang refuses it outright and states his own position: God is perfection and creator, and gives freedom to the universe as an expression of unconditional love.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student objection answered by Jiang monologue

interactions.summary: Two students press the parental analogy by saying real parents impose responsibilities and do not let children do whatever they want, and Jiang answers that free will still operates inside a universe with rules and limits.
A student raises the Eden problem, asking whether Adam and Eve lacked the knowledge required for free will and whether freedom was taken, imposed, or introduced through deception.

speaker_notes.note: The father's objection is noisy in the ASR, but the intended point is clear: loving a child can include correction and responsibility, not simple noninterference.

claims.claim: Jiang rejects the idea that God is fundamentally a judge and instead defines God as perfection and creator whose way of loving the universe is to grant it freedom.
Jiang says God does not command humans toward good, evil, or even aspiration toward God, because free will itself is the ultimate law through which divine love is expressed.
Jiang clarifies that human freedom is not limitless omnipotence, because God also sets rules and boundaries within the universe.
A student question now introduced for later resolution is whether the Eden story implies that free will required knowledge of good and evil or was somehow forced on humanity through deception.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang hardens the lecture's core thesis into a cosmological axiom: free will is the ultimate law because it is how God loves.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Free will is the ultimate law of the universe
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet where the love analogy becomes a full theological model rather than a passing classroom illustration.

signature_moments.moment: God is described not as authority demanding compliance but as a being whose entire existence is ordered toward love.
signature_moments.source_phrase: God exists. He exists. He exists to love you
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The repetition gives emotional force to Jiang's refusal of punitive or merely legal pictures of the divine.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang protects the free-will thesis from a lazy libertarian reading by saying the universe still has real limits.
signature_moments.source_phrase: There are rules to the universe
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps freedom from collapsing into omnipotent license and preserves Dante's ordered cosmos.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's name for free will when he treats it as the deepest structure of reality and the primary expression of divine love.
The classroom tests whether unconditional love means noninterference or support within limits, and Jiang uses the term to ground his theology of free will.

chronology_notes.note: This packet crystallizes the lecture's current position: freedom is an expression of divine love within an ordered universe, and the Eden problem is introduced as the next pressure point rather than left outside the model.

uncertainty_notes.note: The opening line of seg-0233 is muddied by overlapping speech, but the functional move is clear: a student is still trying to preserve the judge analogy and Jiang immediately cuts it off.
